piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: No age is closed to great intellects, and there is no time that is not open to thought
piece.follows: No age is closed to a great intellect; all of time is open to thought.
piece.context: In Letter 102 Seneca lets the soul speak for itself: it will not put up with a narrow span of life and claims all the years as its own.
gives: I take the wide view

items.label: practice
items.t: When I want to know what a person is truly worth, I look at them stripped: in my mind I set aside their estate, their offices and fortune’s other lies, and even the body. Otherwise I am measuring the pedestal along with the person, and a dwarf is not great for standing on a mountain.
items.why: Marcus says what to look at, the soul, and the article sums up what he sets aside as fame and power. He gives no way of looking. Seneca gives one, and it sets aside more: estate, offices and the body itself. “Otherwise” is the editor’s join: in Letter 76 the pedestal (76.31) comes just before the stripping (76.32). “In my mind” is the editor’s: Seneca’s “naked” is a figure for setting fortune’s gifts aside in judging.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: when you want to make a true valuation of a human being and to know what he is like, examine him naked; let him lay aside his estate, let him lay aside his offices and the other lies of fortune, let him strip off even his body
support.follows: To learn a man’s true worth, look at him without his estate, his offices, fortune’s other lies and even his body.
support.context: Letter 76 argues that the honourable is the only good. Here Seneca gives a way to learn a man’s true worth; “naked” means without what fortune has lent him.
gives: When I want to know what a person is truly worth, I look at them stripped: in my mind I set aside their estate, their offices and fortune’s other lies, and even the body

support.author: seneca
support.quote: You are measuring him together with his pedestal. A dwarf is not great though he has taken his stand on a mountain
support.follows: A man raised high seems great because the pedestal is measured with him; a dwarf on a mountain is still not great.
support.context: Letter 76: Seneca asks why those raised high by riches and offices seem great to Lucilius. The “pedestal” is the wealth and office such a man stands on.
gives: I am measuring the pedestal along with the person, and a dwarf is not great for standing on a mountain

items.label: practice
items.t: I choose someone whose life and speech have pleased me and show that person to myself always as my example, for what is crooked cannot be straightened without a ruler. If I want an example, I can take Socrates.
items.why: The section is Marcus’s own gallery of models, Socrates first, but no passage in it says to choose a model and keep him in view. Seneca states the practice and names the same man. He recommends Socrates for his endurance, which is part of what 7.37 says is not enough to judge him by.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Choose the man whose life and speech and very face, which carries his mind in plain view, have pleased you. Show him to yourself always, either as guardian or as example.
support.follows: I should choose a person whose life and speech please me and keep him before me as my guardian or example.
support.context: Seneca ends Letter 11 with a saying of Epicurus: keep a man of high character before your eyes. He suggests Cato or Laelius; “the man” means such a model.
gives: I choose someone whose life and speech have pleased me and show that person to myself always as my example

support.author: seneca
support.quote: you will not straighten what is crooked except against a ruler
support.follows: What is crooked can be straightened only against a ruler.
support.context: The last sentence of Letter 11, giving the reason for choosing a model: we need someone against whom our character may measure itself. The “ruler” is that person.
gives: what is crooked cannot be straightened without a ruler

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If, however, you people want an example, take Socrates
support.follows: Anyone who wants an example can take Socrates.
support.context: In Letter 104 Seneca offers an example to those who want one and goes on to recount Socrates’ poverty, soldiering, harsh home, the Thirty Tyrants, his trial and the poison.
gives: If I want an example, I can take Socrates

items.label: why
items.t: Birth is not the measure either. Socrates was not a patrician, and a hall full of ancestors’ images does not make anyone noble: it is the mind that does that, whatever station a person started from.
items.why: The article sets aside fame and power, and in 1.8 Marcus notes that patricians tend to lack affection, but no passage of the section says that birth is not the measure. Seneca says it, and gives the word “noble” to the mind. The first sentence, “Birth is not the measure either”, is the editor’s summary of the three quotes and is backed by none alone.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Socrates was not a patrician.
support.follows: Socrates was not of noble birth.
support.context: Letter 44 tells Lucilius, a Roman knight, that a noble mind is open to everyone and philosophy asks no pedigree. Socrates heads a list of philosophers of humble origin.
gives: Socrates was not a patrician

support.author: seneca
support.quote: A hall full of smoke-darkened images of ancestors does not make a man noble.
support.follows: A hall full of old ancestor images does not make a man noble.
support.context: Letter 44: Seneca asks who is well born and answers: the man who is well made by nature for virtue. The images are the ancestor portraits kept in the hall of a noble Roman house.
gives: a hall full of ancestors’ images does not make anyone noble

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is the mind that makes a man noble, and from any station whatever the mind may rise above fortune
support.follows: It is the mind that makes us noble, and it can rise above fortune from any station.
support.context: Letter 44, on pedigrees: no life lived before ours lends us glory. Here “noble” is the word for high birth, which he gives to the mind instead.
gives: it is the mind that does that, whatever station a person started from

items.label: action
items.t: I ought to be just without payment and without glory. Often I shall have to be just with a bad name.
items.why: 7.26 and 7.37 say that being just is enough; neither says it may cost me my good name. Seneca names that cost: no payment, no glory, and often a bad name. His “bad name” means being ill spoken of. It is not the disgrace of 7.26, which is the shame of doing wrong, so the two do not conflict.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let each person convince himself of this before everything: I ought to be just without payment.
support.follows: Before everything else each person should be convinced that he ought to be just without payment.
support.context: The end of Letter 113, where Seneca says what he wants to be taught about justice: it looks to another’s good and seeks nothing for itself. Here “each person” includes himself.
gives: I ought to be just without payment

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Are you unwilling to be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name
support.follows: I should be willing to be just without glory, and shall often have to be just with a bad name.
support.context: Seneca’s last words to Lucilius in Letter 113. A “bad name” here means being ill spoken of: the sentence goes on to call it a bad reputation, well won, and a delight to the wise.
gives: without glory
Often I shall have to be just with a bad name

items.label: action
items.t: I live as long as I ought, not merely as long as it pleases me. Sometimes I must hold on to life, even with torment, for the sake of my own people.
items.why: 7.26 tells me to let go of how long I live and leaves the length to god. Seneca, who elsewhere lets a wise man choose his hour (Letter 70), here gives the duty to stay for those who need me; only that half is used, since choosing one’s hour runs against 7.26.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the good man must live not as long as it pleases him but as long as he ought
support.follows: A good man must live as long as he ought, not as long as it pleases him.
support.context: Letter 104: Seneca, old and ill, says he looks after his health for the sake of his wife Paulina, whose life hangs on his. Living “as long as he ought” here means living on for those who need him.
gives: I live as long as I ought, not merely as long as it pleases me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the breath must be called back, even with torment, out of regard for one’s own people, and held back in the very mouth
support.follows: Sometimes life must be held on to, even with torment, for the sake of one’s own people.
support.context: From Letter 104, where Seneca explains why he nurses his health: his wife Paulina asks it. The man who persists in dying when his own people need him he calls soft.
gives: Sometimes I must hold on to life, even with torment, for the sake of my own people

items.label: breaks
items.t: A free person can be a slave: one to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and everyone to fear. The conquerors were themselves conquered, by desire, and while they seemed to be driving others they were themselves being driven: Alexander by a madness for laying waste what belonged to others, Pompey by a love of false greatness, Gaius Caesar by the wish to stand above everyone.
items.why: 8.3 exclaims “slavery to how many!” and does not say to what. Seneca takes the same three men, Alexander, Pompey and Gaius Caesar, and names what drove each. In Letter 94 his words are “conquered” and “driven”; the word “slave” for such masters is from Letter 47.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Show who is not one: one man is a slave to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, [gap in the Latin] all to fear.
support.follows: No one is free of slavery: one serves lust, another greed, another ambition, and all serve fear.
support.context: Letter 47 asks Lucilius to treat his slaves as people. To the objection “He is a slave” Seneca answers that free men have masters of their own. Here “not one” means not a slave.
gives: A free person can be a slave: one to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and everyone to fear

support.author: seneca
support.quote: these too, in order to conquer the enemy, were conquered by desire
support.follows: In order to conquer their enemies, these men too were conquered by desire.
support.context: Letter 94: Seneca describes the voice that should warn us against envying those the people call great. Here “these” are generals who storm cities and reach the sea in blood.
gives: The conquerors were themselves conquered, by desire

support.author: seneca
support.quote: neither had they themselves withstood ambition and cruelty; at the time when they seemed to be driving others, they were being driven
support.follows: They had not withstood their own ambition and cruelty; while they seemed to drive others, they were driven themselves.
support.context: Letter 94, on generals who sack cities and whom no one withstood. Here “they” are those generals, the men the people call great and fortunate.
gives: while they seemed to be driving others they were themselves being driven

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Wretched Alexander was driven by a madness for laying waste what belonged to others, and it sent him off to unknown lands.
support.follows: Wretched Alexander was driven, and sent into unknown lands, by a madness for laying waste what belonged to others.
support.context: The first of Seneca’s examples in Letter 94 of men the crowd calls great who were driven, not driving. He goes on to Alexander’s ruin of Greece.
gives: Alexander by a madness for laying waste what belonged to others

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Gnaeus Pompeius, too, was urged to wars abroad and at home not by virtue or reason but by an insane love of false greatness.
support.follows: What took Pompey into his wars was not virtue or reason but an insane love of false greatness.
support.context: Seneca’s second example in Letter 94, after Alexander, of a conqueror driven by his own desire. He calls the causes given for Pompey’s campaigns a cover for keeping his power unbroken.
gives: Pompey by a love of false greatness

support.author: seneca
support.quote: What sent Gaius Caesar headlong into his own doom and the state’s alike? Glory and ambition and no limit to standing out above the rest.
support.follows: What sent Gaius Caesar into his own doom and the state’s was glory, ambition and a limitless wish to stand out above the rest.
support.context: Seneca’s third example in Letter 94 of a great man driven by his own desires. This Gaius Caesar is Julius Caesar, who could not let anyone outrank him.
gives: Gaius Caesar by the wish to stand above everyone

items.t: Seneca agrees that fame is not the measure and that talk does not show the strength of a mind: in Letter 26 he sets aside the estimate people make. Marcus says that the glory of a death, how it was seen by others, is not enough to show that Socrates was the better man. Seneca says that how one meets death is the proof of a mind’s true strength: what a person has done shows at the last breath. He says this to himself and then to Lucilius; applying it to any soul is the editor’s step. He reads Socrates in the same way, from his trials, which did not move his mind (Ep. 104.28). He also trusts that virtue comes to light in the end, though he adds that being hidden is no loss to it (Ep. 79.17); Marcus leaves open that the better man may be one nobody knows. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: for both, the soul is the measure; Marcus sets aside the glory of a death, and Seneca looks to the conduct in it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: death is going to pronounce on you
support.follows: It is death that will pronounce on me.
support.context: Letter 26: Seneca, in old age, tells himself that his words so far prove nothing about him. Here “you” is himself, and he then offers the same words to Lucilius.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: What you have done will be seen at the moment when you breathe your last.
support.follows: What I have really done will be seen when I breathe my last.
support.context: From Letter 26, on old age and death: debates and learned talk do not show the true strength of the mind. Here “you” is Seneca addressing himself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So far had these things been from moving the mind of Socrates that they did not move even his face.
support.follows: Everything done to Socrates moved his mind so little that it did not move even his face.
support.context: Letter 104: Seneca’s portrait of Socrates as an example. Here “these things” are the long war, the Thirty Tyrants, the charges against him, the prison and the poison.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: No virtue lies hidden, and to have lain hidden is not virtue’s own loss: a day will come to make public the virtue that was buried
support.follows: Virtue does not stay hidden, and being hidden costs it nothing; a day will come that makes it public.
support.context: Letter 79: fame follows virtue like a shadow, sometimes late; Democritus, Socrates and Cato were recognised slowly. The virtue “that was buried” is the one its own age held down out of spite.

amend.t: ; to see that soul I set aside, in my mind, the estate, the offices and even the body
; yet how a person meets death does judge their soul: what they have done shows at the last breath

passages.title: On choosing the right time to die
passages.text: Consider that the same happens to us: life has brought some very quickly to the place that even those who hang back had to come to, and others it has soaked and stewed. Life, as you know, is not always to be held on to. For it is not living that is a good, but living well. So the wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can.

passages.title: On a friend’s calm, chosen death
passages.text: Our Stoic friend, an outstanding person and, to praise him in the words in which he deserves to be praised, a brave and energetic man, seems to me to have urged him on best. For he began like this: “Do not torment yourself, my Marcellinus, as if you were deliberating about a great matter. Living is not a great matter: all your slaves live, all animals do. The great thing is to die honourably, sensibly, bravely. Think how long you have now been doing the same thing: food, sleep, lust. This is the circle one runs round. Not only a sensible man or a brave one or a wretched one can want to die, but also one who is jaded.”

passages.title: On learning in old age, and virtue as the only good
passages.text: This is the error we suffer from, this is how we are taken in: we value no one by what he is, but add to him the things he is decked out with as well. Yet when you want to make a true valuation of a human being and to know what he is like, examine him naked; let him lay aside his estate, let him lay aside his offices and the other lies of fortune, let him strip off even his body: look at his mind, what it is like and how great, whether it is great by what is another’s or by what is its own.

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Fix in yourself as well what I was saying a little earlier: that it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness. Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory. Are you unwilling to be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name, and then, if you are wise, let a bad reputation well won delight you. Farewell.

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Let him teach me how sacred a thing justice is, which looks to another’s good and asks nothing from itself except to be put to use. Let it have nothing to do with ambition and reputation: let it win its own approval. Let each person convince himself of this before everything: I ought to be just without payment. That is too little. Let him convince himself of this as well: let me be glad to go further and even spend on this most beautiful virtue; let all thought be turned as far as possible away from private advantages. There is no reason for you to look to what the reward of a just act is: there is a greater one in what is just.

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul’s immortality
passages.text: Say rather how natural it is to stretch one’s mind out into what has no measure. The human soul is a great and noble thing. It lets no boundaries be set for it except those it shares with god as well. First, it does not accept a lowly homeland, Ephesus or Alexandria or any ground there may be that is still more crowded with inhabitants or richer in buildings. Its homeland is whatever encloses the highest things and the whole of things in its circuit: this entire vault within which the seas and the lands lie, within which the air, while it separates the divine from the human, also joins them, in which so many divine powers are posted and stand watch, ready for their own work.

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul’s immortality
passages.text: Next, it does not let a narrow span of life be given to it. “All the years are mine,” it says. “No age is closed to great intellects, and there is no time that is not open to thought. When that day comes which is to separate this mixture of the divine and the human, I will leave the body here where I found it, and myself I will give back to the gods. Even now I am not without them, but I am held back by what is heavy and earthly.”

passages.title: On learning in old age, and virtue as the only good
passages.text: None of those whom you see dressed in purple is happy, any more than any of those to whom the plays assign a sceptre and a cloak on the stage: when they have walked before the people with a broad swagger and in high boots, they have no sooner made their exit than their boots are taken off and they return to their own stature. None of those whom riches and offices set at a greater height is great. Why then does he seem great? You are measuring him together with his pedestal. A dwarf is not great though he has taken his stand on a mountain; a colossus will keep its greatness even if it stands in a well.

passages.title: On blushing and choosing a role model
passages.text: So choose Cato. If he seems to you too stiff, choose Laelius, a man of a more relaxed mind. Choose the man whose life and speech and very face, which carries his mind in plain view, have pleased you. Show him to yourself always, either as guardian or as example. Someone is needed, I say, against whom our character may measure itself: you will not straighten what is crooked except against a ruler. Farewell.

passages.title: On travel, health and the examples of great men
passages.text: If, however, you people want an example, take Socrates, a long-suffering old man, tossed through every hardship, yet unconquered both by poverty, which his household burdens made heavier for him, and by toils, which he bore in military service as well. By these he was harassed at home, whether [one thinks of] his wife, with her savage ways and abusive tongue, or [of] his children, unteachable and more like their mother than their father; [the text is damaged here] he lived either in war or under tyranny or in a freedom crueller than wars and tyrants.

passages.title: On true nobility coming from the mind
passages.text: Socrates was not a patrician. Cleanthes drew water and hired out his hands for watering a garden. Philosophy did not receive Plato as a noble; it made him one. Why should you despair of being able to become the equal of these men? All of these are your ancestors, if you conduct yourself in a way worthy of them; and you will, if you persuade yourself of this at once: that you are surpassed by no one in nobility.

passages.title: On true nobility coming from the mind
passages.text: Who is well born? The man who is well made by nature for virtue. This is the one thing to look at. Otherwise, if you go back to ancient times, there is no one who does not come from that point before which there is nothing. From the first beginning of the world down to this time we have been led all the way by a line in which the splendid and the lowly alternate. A hall full of smoke-darkened images of ancestors does not make a man noble. No one has lived for our glory, and what was before us is not ours. It is the mind that makes a man noble, and from any station whatever the mind may rise above fortune.

passages.title: On travel, health and the examples of great men
passages.text: For one must indulge honourable feelings; and sometimes, even if there are pressing reasons, the breath must be called back, even with torment, out of regard for one’s own people, and held back in the very mouth, since the good man must live not as long as it pleases him but as long as he ought. The man who thinks neither a wife nor a friend worth so much that he would stay longer in life, who will persist in dying, is soft. This too the mind should command of itself, when the interest of its own people demands it: not only if it wants to die but if it has begun to, it should pause and oblige its own people.

passages.title: On treating slaves as fellow humans
passages.text: “He is a slave.” But perhaps free in mind. “He is a slave.” Will that harm him? Show who is not one: one man is a slave to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, [gap in the Latin] all to fear. I will give you a man of consular rank who is a slave to a little old woman, I will give you a rich man who is a slave to a slave girl, I will show you young men of the noblest birth who are the bought slaves of pantomime dancers: no slavery is more shameful than voluntary slavery. So there is no reason why those disdainful people should deter you from showing yourself cheerful to your slaves, and superior without being arrogant: let them honour you rather than fear you.

passages.title: On the usefulness of practical advice
passages.text: Many are found who carry fire into cities, who lay low what the centuries could not storm and what had been safe through several generations, who raise a siege mound level with citadels, and with rams and engines batter walls that had been built up to an astonishing height. There are many who drive armies before them and press hard on the backs of the enemy and come to the great sea drenched in the slaughter of nations; but these too, in order to conquer the enemy, were conquered by desire. No one withstood them as they came, but neither had they themselves withstood ambition and cruelty; at the time when they seemed to be driving others, they were being driven.

passages.title: On the usefulness of practical advice
passages.text: Wretched Alexander was driven by a madness for laying waste what belonged to others, and it sent him off to unknown lands. Or do you think a man sane who begins by bringing disasters first on Greece, where he was educated? Who snatches from each the best thing it has: orders Sparta to be a slave, Athens to be silent? Not content with the overthrow of so many states, which Philip had either conquered or bought, he throws down others, some in one place and some in another, and carries his arms around the whole world; and nowhere does his cruelty tire and come to a halt, like savage beasts that bite more than hunger demands.

passages.title: On the usefulness of practical advice
passages.text: Gnaeus Pompeius, too, was urged to wars abroad and at home not by virtue or reason but by an insane love of false greatness. Now he was going into Spain and against the arms of Sertorius, now to bind the pirates and pacify the seas: these were the causes held out as a cover for keeping his power unbroken.

passages.title: On the usefulness of practical advice
passages.text: What dragged him into Africa, what into the north, what against Mithridates and into Armenia and every corner of Asia? Plainly a boundless desire to grow, since to himself alone he seemed not great enough. What sent Gaius Caesar headlong into his own doom and the state’s alike? Glory and ambition and no limit to standing out above the rest. He could not bear one man ahead of him, though the state was bearing two above it.

passages.title: On old age, and death as the test of progress
passages.text: Set aside the estimate people make: it is always uncertain and is split both ways. Set aside the studies you have pursued all your life: death is going to pronounce on you. This is what I say: debates, literary conversations, words collected from the teachings of the wise, and learned talk do not show the true strength of the mind; for even the most timid have bold speech. What you have done will be seen at the moment when you breathe your last. I accept the terms; I do not shrink from the judgment.”

passages.title: On travel, health and the examples of great men
passages.text: There was fighting for twenty-seven years. After the war was ended the city was given up to be harmed by thirty tyrants, most of whom were his enemies. Last of all, his condemnation was carried through under the gravest charges: he was accused both of violating religion and of corrupting the young, whom he was said to be letting loose against the gods, against their fathers, against the state. After this, prison and poison. So far had these things been from moving the mind of Socrates that they did not move even his face. What a wonderful and unique distinction that is! To the very end no one saw Socrates more cheerful or more gloomy; he was unvarying amid such great variation of fortune.

passages.title: On Etna, virtue and late fame
passages.text: No virtue lies hidden, and to have lain hidden is not virtue’s own loss: a day will come to make public the virtue that was buried and held down by the spite of its own age. The man who thinks of the people of his own time is born for few. Many thousands of years, many thousands of peoples will come after: look to those. Even if envy has imposed silence on all who are alive with you, there will come those who judge without ill will, without favour. If virtue has any reward from fame, this does not perish either. The talk of those who come after will indeed not concern us at all; yet it will honour us and keep returning to us even though we do not feel it.

claims.t: Staying alive is not the great thing, and dying is not the worst thing. Where I have taken up a post I stay and run the risk, and I weigh nothing, not even death, against doing what is shameful.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of life and of death and give neither the first place. In 7.26 Socrates asks the other man to see whether what is noble and good “may not be something other” than “saving and being saved”, and says that “neither death nor anything else” counts ahead of disgrace. In 7.23 human life does not seem “anything great”, and death is not counted “a terrible thing”.
claims.changed: 7.26 is about a man at his post and 7.23 about a mind that has all of time in view; the claim keeps the two judgments they share and adds the post from 7.26 alone. “Dying is not the worst thing” is the least that both say: 7.26 puts disgrace ahead of death, and 7.23 goes further and says that death is not a terrible thing; neither of these is hedged. “Staying alive is not the great thing” rests on 7.23’s question about life and on 7.26’s third paragraph, which is hedged (“see whether … may not be”, “perhaps”); the article reads the hedge as Socrates’ polite way of asserting. 7.23 makes both judgments only of a mind with a view of all time, a condition the claim drops. “Doing what is shameful” follows the translators’ other reading of 7.26’s “ahead of disgrace” (Greek “before the shameful”): the disgrace meant is the shameful act, not the loss of a good name.

support.quote: see whether what is noble and what is good may not be something other than saving and being saved. For perhaps this, living for whatever length of time, is what one who is truly a man must let go, and he must not cling to life
support.follows: What is noble and good may be something other than staying alive, and perhaps a true man must let go of how long he lives.
gives: Staying alive is not the great thing

support.quote: do you think human life seems anything great to the one who has it?’ ‘Impossible,’ he said.
support.follows: To a mind with a view of all time and of all being, human life cannot seem anything great.
gives: Staying alive is not the great thing

support.quote: Wherever a person has taken up a post, judging it to be best, or has been posted by a commander, there, as it seems to me, they must stay and run the risk, taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, ahead of disgrace
support.follows: Whoever has taken up a post, or been posted there, must stay and run the risk, counting nothing, death included, ahead of disgrace.
gives: dying is not the worst thing
Where I have taken up a post I stay and run the risk, and I weigh nothing, not even death, against doing what is shameful

support.quote: such a person will not count death a terrible thing either
support.follows: Whoever has a view of all time and of all being will not count death a terrible thing.
gives: dying is not the worst thing

claims.t: I measure a person by the kind of soul they have. It is not power that counts: Alexander, Gaius Caesar and Pompey are little beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates. And it is not fame: for all I know, Telauges was a better man than Socrates, though hardly anyone has heard of him. Not even Socrates’ more glorious death is enough to show which of the two was better.
claims.shared: 7.37 and 8.3 both set Socrates beside other men and both look inside for the difference: 7.37 at “what kind of soul Socrates had”, 8.3 at the philosophers’ “ruling parts”. In both, what the world saw of a man is not what decides: Socrates’ glorious death in 7.37, the three conquerors in 8.3.
claims.changed: “I measure” is the editor’s word for 7.37’s “what has to be looked at” and 8.3’s “what are they beside”. 8.3 says “ruling parts”, the part of the soul that governs; the claim says “soul”, 7.37’s word. The text of 8.3’s “their ruling parts were the same” may be faulty, but the claim uses it only to say that 8.3 looks inside the men, which holds on either reading. The Greek of 8.3 has only “Gaius”; the translators’ note says he is Gaius Julius Caesar, and the claim writes “Gaius Caesar” so that he is not taken for the emperor Caligula. Neither “fame” nor “power” is a word of the passages: “fame” sums up 7.37’s list of what was seen and told of Socrates, “power” what Alexander, Gaius and Pompey have in common.

inferences.words: though hardly anyone has heard of him
inferences.why: 7.37 names Telauges and says nothing about him. The gloss is the editor’s, from the translators’ note that he stands for a man of whom little is known.

support.quote: what has to be looked at is this: what kind of soul Socrates had
support.follows: The thing to look at in Socrates is what kind of soul he had.
gives: I measure a person by the kind of soul they have

support.quote: For the latter saw things and their causes and their matter, and their ruling parts were the same.
support.follows: The reason given for setting the philosophers higher is what they saw and the state of their ruling parts.
gives: by the kind of soul they have

support.quote: Alexander, Gaius and Pompey: what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates?
support.follows: Alexander, Gaius and Pompey amount to little when set beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates.
gives: It is not power that counts: Alexander, Gaius Caesar and Pompey are little beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates

support.quote: it is not enough that Socrates died a more glorious death, and argued more nimbly with the sophists
support.follows: A more glorious death and more skill in argument are not enough to show that Socrates was the better man.
gives: it is not fame
Not even Socrates’ more glorious death is enough to show which of the two was better

support.quote: How do we know that Telauges was not better than Socrates in his disposition?
support.follows: We do not know that Telauges was not the better man in his inner disposition.
gives: for all I know, Telauges was a better man than Socrates

claims.t: Being just is enough for me: when I act I look at this alone, whether what I am doing is just or unjust, and I ask no more of myself than to be just in my dealings with people and devout in my dealings with the gods.
claims.shared: Both passages name being just, and both say that nothing more is needed: 7.26 tells a man to “look at this alone”, whether what he does is “just or unjust”; 7.37 asks whether Socrates could “find it enough to be just”.
claims.changed: 7.26 is Socrates speaking of any man who is of use; 7.37 is a question about Socrates, not a statement. The claim says “I” and turns the question into a resolve. 7.37 puts being devout towards the gods beside being just towards people; the claim keeps it, although 7.26 does not say it.

support.quote: look at this alone whenever he acts: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one
support.follows: Whenever a man acts he should look at one thing only: whether what he is doing is just or unjust.
gives: Being just is enough for me
when I act I look at this alone, whether what I am doing is just or unjust
I ask no more of myself than to be just

support.quote: whether he could find it enough to be just in his dealings with human beings and devout in his dealings with the gods
support.follows: The question about Socrates is whether being just to people and devout to the gods was enough for him.
gives: Being just is enough for me
I ask no more of myself than to be just in my dealings with people and devout in my dealings with the gods

claims.t: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong: I do not get idly angry at vice, and I do not fight and fall out with them.
claims.shared: 7.37 and 1.7 both meet another person’s fault and both refuse the hostile answer: 7.37 has “neither getting idly angry at vice”, 1.7 “not to pounce reproachfully” on someone’s mistake. 11.32 asks people who say their souls are sound why they “fight and fall out”. The three have no word in common; what they share is the refusal.
claims.changed: 1.7 is about slips in speech and 7.37 about vice; the claim covers anything a person gets wrong. “I do not turn on people” is the editor’s summary of the two. 11.32 says nothing about faults and backs only the last words. 11.32 is a question put to people who quarrel among themselves, and 7.37 a question about Socrates; the claim turns both into a resolve, “I do not …”, and “with them”, the people who get things wrong, is the object the editor gives to 11.32’s fighting.

support.quote: neither getting idly angry at vice
support.follows: The soul this passage asks about does not get angry at vice to no purpose.
gives: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong
I do not get idly angry at vice

support.quote: not to find fault, and not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with a wrong form of a word, a mistake in grammar or a jarring sound
support.follows: From Alexander the grammarian: not to find fault with people or pounce on them for a slip in their speech.
gives: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong

support.quote: “Sound ones.” “Then why do you not look for them?” “Because we have them.” “Then why do you fight and fall out?”
support.follows: Socrates asks people who say they already have sound souls why, then, they fight and fall out.
gives: I do not fight and fall out with them

claims.t: I take the wide view: of all time and all that exists, and of the things on earth as if from somewhere above. I look round at the courses of the stars and think continually of the elements changing into one another; picturing these things washes away the dirt of life down here on the ground.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of looking at far more than what is in front of me: 7.23 of a mind with “a view of all time and of all being”, 7.26 of looking round at the stars and looking down at the things on earth “as if from somewhere above”.
claims.changed: 7.26 gives instructions; 7.23 describes a mind that has such a view and does not say how to get it. The claim makes one exercise of them. “The wide view” is the editor’s name for what the two describe. 7.26’s list of what is seen from above, from herds to markets, is left out. “Picturing these things” is the translators’ other reading of 7.26’s “the impressions of these things”, and “down here” is added to set the ground against the stars, as the translators’ note does.

support.quote: a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of all being
support.follows: There is a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of everything that exists.
gives: I take the wide view
of all time and all that exists

support.quote: whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above
support.follows: Anyone who talks about human beings should also look down at earthly things as if from above.
gives: I take the wide view
of the things on earth as if from somewhere above

support.quote: Look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and think continually of the changes of the elements into one another. For the impressions of these things wash away the dirt of life on the ground.
support.follows: Picturing the stars’ courses and the elements changing into one another washes away the dirt of life on earth.
gives: I take the wide view
I look round at the courses of the stars and think continually of the elements changing into one another; picturing these things washes away the dirt of life down here on the ground

claims.t: I shall not be a slave: not to another person’s ignorance, and not as Alexander, Gaius Caesar and Pompey were, who had so many things to take thought for and were slaves to so many.
claims.shared: Both passages use the word: 7.37 has “being a slave to anyone’s ignorance”, 8.3 “slavery to how many!” In both it is what marks off the worse soul from the better one.
claims.changed: 8.3 exclaims over the conquerors and gives no instruction, and 7.37 asks whether Socrates was free of it; “I shall not be” is the editor’s turn of both into a resolve. 8.3 does not say whether the conquerors were slaves to things or to people. 8.3’s last sentence says only “the others”; the names are those 8.3 gives in its first sentence.

support.quote: nor yet being a slave to anyone’s ignorance
support.follows: The soul this passage asks about is not a slave to anyone’s ignorance.
gives: I shall not be a slave
not to another person’s ignorance

support.quote: But with the others, how many things to take thought for, and slavery to how many!
support.follows: The others, the three conquerors, had a great many things to take thought for and were slaves to a great many.
gives: I shall not be a slave
not as Alexander, Gaius Caesar and Pompey were, who had so many things to take thought for and were slaves to so many

single.quote: Nature did not blend the mind with the compound in such a way that it is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself and to bring what is its own under its own control.
single.label: The mind’s own boundary
single.t: Nature did not blend my mind with my body in such a way that it cannot draw a boundary round itself and bring what is its own under its own control.
single.why: Only this passage says that the mind can draw a boundary round itself. It gives a ground for a mind that is not a slave, but it does not use that word and it speaks of the body, so it is not joined to the claim about slavery.
single.follows: The mind is not so mixed with the compound it lives in that it cannot mark itself off and take charge of what is its own.

single.quote: Socrates used to call the principles of the many, too, “Lamias”, things to frighten children.
single.label: Bogeys
single.t: When the principles most people live by frighten me, I remember that Socrates used to call them “Lamias”, things to frighten children.
single.why: Only this passage gives the saying, and it does not say which principles are meant. Turning the saying into something I recall when such principles frighten me is the editor’s turn.
single.follows: Socrates called what most people hold and live by “Lamias”, things that frighten children.

single.quote: leaving these matters to god and trusting the women who say that not even one person could escape what is fated, he must consider what comes next: how he might best live the time he is going to live
single.label: The next question
single.t: How long I shall live I leave to god. I consider what comes next: how to live the time I am going to live as well as possible.
single.why: Only this passage turns from how long I live to how well. Socrates puts it guardedly (“perhaps … must”); the item reads that as his polite way of asserting and states it as my resolve, which is the editor’s turn. The trust in “the women who say” that no one escapes what is fated is left out.
single.follows: Perhaps a true man must leave the length of his life to god and ask how to live the time he has as well as possible.

single.quote: not to say “I am busy” to anyone, or write it in a letter, often or without need; and not to keep excusing oneself in this way from the duties that come with one’s relations to those one lives among, by pleading the business that surrounds one
single.label: “I am busy”
single.t: I shall not say or write “I am busy” often or without need, and I shall not keep pleading my business to excuse myself from what I owe the people I live among.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of being busy. 7.37 asks for justice towards people in general; this names one way of failing the people nearest to me.
single.follows: From Alexander the Platonist: seldom to say “I am busy”, and not to plead business to get out of duties to those one lives among.

single.quote: Socrates to Perdiccas, on not going to him: “So that I may not die the worst of deaths,” he said, that is, so that I may not, after receiving a kindness, be unable to do one in return.
single.label: A kindness I cannot return
single.t: I keep in mind why Socrates would not go to King Perdiccas: so that he would not receive a kindness and be unable to do one in return, which he called the worst of deaths.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of returning a kindness. Marcus gives the saying under a heading and draws no rule from it, so the item keeps it as a reason to remember; “I keep in mind” is the editor’s turn. “King” is from the translators’ note.
single.follows: Socrates would not go to Perdiccas, so as not to receive a kindness he could not return, which he called the worst of deaths.

single.quote: deftly to come out with just the very thing that should have been said, by way of an answer, or of backing them up, or of a joint discussion about the matter itself, not about the expression
single.label: Correcting without reproach
single.t: When someone says a thing wrongly, I come out with the right form myself: in my answer, in backing them up, or in talking with them about the matter itself, not the wording.
single.why: Only this passage says how to correct someone. The first half of 1.7 goes into the claim about other people’s faults; this half is the exercise.
single.follows: From Alexander the grammarian: to correct a slip by deftly using the right form oneself, in an answer or in discussing the matter.

single.quote: to have taken note of what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that on the whole these people we call patricians are somehow rather lacking in affection
single.label: What a tyrant is like
single.t: I keep in mind what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that the people we call patricians are, on the whole, rather lacking in affection.
single.why: Only this passage describes the tyrant and the patricians. Marcus records what he noticed and draws no rule; “I keep in mind” is the editor’s turn. It stands under this label as a picture of what power and high birth can make of a soul, not as a failing of my own.
single.follows: From Fronto: to have noticed what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that patricians are on the whole rather lacking in affection.

single.quote: Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver, once dead, came to the same state: for either they were taken back into the same seed-reasons of the universe, or they were scattered alike into atoms.
single.label: The king and the mule driver
single.t: Whichever account of the world is true, Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver came to the same state once they were dead: either both were taken back into the reason that runs the universe, from which all things grow, or both were scattered alike into atoms.
single.why: Only this passage argues by cases, and it is about what death does, not about how to measure a person, so it is not joined to the claim that names Alexander. It says what holds on either account of the world, a universe run by reason or one of atoms only. The item gives the plain sense of the Stoic term “seed-reasons”, as the translators’ note explains it.
single.follows: Once dead, the king and the man who drove his mules were in the same state, whether the universe took them back or they were scattered into atoms.

members.text:
Out of Plato. 'My answer, full of justice and equity, should be
this: Thy speech is not right, O man! if thou supposest that he that is
of any worth at all, should apprehend either life or death, as a matter
of great hazard and danger; and should not make this rather his only
care, to examine his own actions, whether just or unjust: whether
actions of a good, or of a wicked man, &c. For thus in very truth stands
the case, O ye men of Athens. What place or station soever a man either
hath chosen to himself, judging it best for himself; or is by lawful
authority put and settled in, therein do I think (all appearance of
danger notwithstanding) that he should continue, as one who feareth
neither death, nor anything else, so much as he feareth to commit
anything that is vicious and shameful, &c. But, O noble sir, consider
I pray, whether true generosity and true happiness, do not consist in
somewhat else rather, than in the preservation either of our, or other
men's lives. For it is not the part of a man that is a man indeed, to
desire to live long or to make much of his life whilst he liveth: but
rather (he that is such) will in these things wholly refer himself unto
the Gods, and believing that which every woman can tell him, that no man
can escape death; the only thing that he takes thought and care for is
this, that what time he liveth, he may live as well and as virtuously
as he can possibly, &c. To look about, and with the eyes to follow the
course of the stars and planets as though thou wouldst run with them;
and to mind perpetually the several changes of the elements one into
another. For such fancies and imaginations, help much to purge away
the dross and filth of this our earthly life,' &c. That also is a fine
passage of Plato's, where he speaketh of worldly things in these words:
'Thou must also as from some higher place look down, as it were, upon
the things of this world, as flocks, armies, husbandmen's labours,
marriages, divorces, generations, deaths: the tumults of courts and
places of judicatures; desert places; the several nations of barbarians,
public festivals, mournings, fairs, markets.' How all things upon earth
are pell-mell; and how miraculously things contrary one to another,
concur to the beauty and perfection of this universe.
members.english:
“But I would have a just answer to give this man: ‘What you say is not right, fellow, if you think that a man who is of even a little use must take into account the risk of living or dying, rather than look at this alone whenever he acts: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one.’”

“For this is how it truly is, men of Athens. Wherever a person has taken up a post, judging it to be best, or has been posted by a commander, there, as it seems to me, they must stay and run the risk, taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, ahead of disgrace.”

“But, my dear man, see whether what is noble and what is good may not be something other than saving and being saved. For perhaps this, living for whatever length of time, is what one who is truly a man must let go, and he must not cling to life. Instead, leaving these matters to god and trusting the women who say that not even one person could escape what is fated, he must consider what comes next: how he might best live the time he is going to live.”

Look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and think continually of the changes of the elements into one another. For the impressions of these things wash away the dirt of life on the ground.

A fine saying of Plato’s. And indeed whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above: herds, armies, farms, marriages, divorces, births, deaths, the din of law courts, empty lands, the varied peoples of the barbarians, festivals, laments, markets, the mixture of every kind and the order put together out of opposites.

Καλὸν τὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος. καὶ δὴ περὶ ἀνθρώπων τοὺς λόγους ποιούμενον ἐπισκοπεῖν δεῖ καὶ τὰ ἐπίγεια ὥσπερ ποθὲν ἄνωθεν κάτω· ἀγέλας, στρατεύματα, γεώργια, γάμους, διαλύσεις, γενέσεις, θανάτους, δικαστηρίων θόρυβον, ἐρήμους χώρας, βαρβάρων ἔθνη ποικίλα, ἑορτάς, θρήνους, ἀγοράς, τὸ παμμιγὲς καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων συγκοσμούμενον.

members.text:
How know we whether Socrates were so eminent indeed, and of so
extraordinary a disposition? For that he died more gloriously, that he
disputed with the Sophists more subtilty; that he watched in the frost
more assiduously; that being commanded to fetch innocent Salaminius, he
refused to do it more generously; all this will not serve. Nor that he
walked in the streets, with much gravity and majesty, as was objected
unto him by his adversaries: which nevertheless a man may well doubt of,
whether it were so or no, or, which above all the rest, if so be that
it were true, a man would well consider of, whether commendable, or
dis-commendable. The thing therefore that we must inquire into, is this;
what manner of soul Socrates had: whether his disposition was such; as
that all that he stood upon, and sought after in this world, was barely
this, that he might ever carry himself justly towards men, and holily
towards the Gods. Neither vexing himself to no purpose at the wickedness
of others, nor yet ever condescending to any man's evil fact, or evil
intentions, through either fear, or engagement of friendship. Whether of
those things that happened unto him by God's appointment, he neither did
wonder at any when it did happen, or thought it intolerable in the trial
of it. And lastly, whether he never did suffer his mind to sympathise
with the senses, and affections of the body. For we must not think that
Nature hath so mixed and tempered it with the body, as that she hath not
power to circumscribe herself, and by herself to intend her own ends and
occasions.
members.english:
How do we know that Telauges was not better than Socrates in his disposition? For it is not enough that Socrates died a more glorious death, and argued more nimbly with the sophists, and showed more endurance in spending the night out in the frost, and, when ordered to bring in the man from Salamis, was thought to have stood against it more nobly, and “swaggered in the streets”, a point one might well take note of most of all, if indeed it was true. But what has to be looked at is this: what kind of soul Socrates had, and whether he could find it enough to be just in his dealings with human beings and devout in his dealings with the gods, neither getting idly angry at vice nor yet being a slave to anyone’s ignorance, neither receiving anything allotted from the whole as something foreign or enduring it as something unbearable, nor handing his mind over to feel with the feelings of the poor flesh.

Nature did not blend the mind with the compound in such a way that it is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself and to bring what is its own under its own control.

Πόθεν ἴσμεν, εἰ μὴ Τηλαύγης Σωκράτους τὴν διάθεσιν κρείσσων ἦν; οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ, εἰ Σωκράτης ἐνδοξότερον ἀπέθανε καὶ ἐντρεχέστερον τοῖς σοφισταῖς διελέγετο καὶ καρτερικώτερον ἐν τῷ πάγῳ διενυκτέρευε καὶ τὸν Σαλαμίνιον κελευσθεὶς ἄγειν γεννικώτερον ἔδοξεν ἀντιβῆναι καὶ ʽἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἐβρενθύετοʼ, περὶ οὗ καὶ μάλιστ’ ἄν τις ἐπιστήσειεν, εἴπερ ἀληθὲς ἦν· ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖνο δεῖ σκοπεῖν, ποίαν τινὰ τὴν ψυχὴν εἶχε Σωκράτης καὶ εἰ ἐδύνατο ἀρκεῖσθαι τῷ δίκαιος εἶναι τὰ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους καὶ ὅσιος τὰ πρὸς θεούς, μήτε εἰκῇ πρὸς τὴν κακίαν ἀγανακτῶν μηδὲ μὴν δουλεύων τινὸς ἀγνοίᾳ, μήτε τῶν ἀπονεμομένων ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου ὡς ξένον τι δεχόμενος ἢ ὡς ἀφόρητον ὑπομένων, μήτε τοῖς τοῦ σαρκιδίου πάθεσιν ἐμπαρέχων συμπαθῆ τὸν νοῦν·

members.text:
Out of Plato. 'He then whose mind is endowed with true
magnanimity, who hath accustomed himself to the contemplation both of
all times, and of all things in general; can this mortal life (thinkest
thou) seem any great matter unto him? It is not possible, answered he.
Then neither will such a one account death a grievous thing? By no
means.'
members.english: “‘So, a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of all being: do you think human life seems anything great to the one who has it?’ ‘Impossible,’ he said. ‘Then such a person will not count death a terrible thing either?’ ‘Not in the least.’”
members.greek: ʽἯι οὖν ὑπάρχει διανοίᾳ μεγαλοπρέπεια καὶ θεωρία παντὸς μὲν χρόνου, πάσης δὲ οὐσίας, ἆρα οἴει τούτῳ μέγα τι δοκεῖν εἶναι τὸν ἀνθρώπινον βίον; ἀδύνατον, ἦ δ’ ὅς. οὐκοῦν καὶ θάνατον οὐ δεινόν τι ἡγήσεται ὁ τοιοῦτος; ἥκιστά γε.ʼ

him, Lest of all deaths I should die the worst kind of death, said he:
that is, not able to requite the good that hath been done unto me.

members.text:
Socrates said, 'What will you have? the souls of
reasonable, or unreasonable creatures? Of reasonable. But what? Of those
whose reason is sound and perfect? or of those whose reason is vitiated
and corrupted? Of those whose reason is sound and perfect. Why then
labour ye not for such? Because we have them already. What then do ye so
strive and contend between you?'
members.english: Socrates used to say: “What do you want? To have the souls of rational beings or of irrational ones?” “Of rational beings.” “Of which rational beings? Sound ones or bad ones?” “Sound ones.” “Then why do you not look for them?” “Because we have them.” “Then why do you fight and fall out?”
members.greek: Ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγε· τί θέλετε; λογικῶν ψυχὰς ἔχειν ἢ ἀλόγων;—λογικῶν.—τίνων λογικῶν; ὑγιῶν ἢ φαύλων;—ὑγιῶν.—τί οὖν οὐ ζητεῖτε;—ὅτι ἔχομεν.—τί οὖν μάχεσθε καὶ διαφέρεσθε;

members.text:
Alexander, Caius, Pompeius; what are these to Diogenes, Heraclitus,
and Socrates? These penetrated into the true nature of things; into all
causes, and all subjects: and upon these did they exercise their power
and authority. But as for those, as the extent of their error was, so
far did their slavery extend.
members.english: And Alexander, Gaius and Pompey: what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates? For the latter saw things and their causes and their matter, and their ruling parts were the same. But with the others, how many things to take thought for, and slavery to how many!
members.greek: Ἀλέξανδρος δὲ καὶ Γάιος καὶ Πομπήιος τί πρὸς Διογένη καὶ Ἡράκλειτον καὶ Σωκράτην; οἱ μὲν γὰρ εἶδον τὰ πράγματα καὶ τὰς αἰτίας καὶ τὰς ὕλας καὶ τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ ἦν αὐτῶν ταὐτά, ἐκεῖ δὲ ὅσων πρόνοια καὶ δουλεία πόσων.

members.text:
Of Alexander the Platonic, not often nor without great necessity to
say, or to write to any man in a letter, 'I am not at leisure'; nor in
this manner still to put off those duties, which we owe to our friends
and acquaintances (to every one in his kind) under pretence of urgent
affairs.
members.english: From Alexander the Platonist: not to say “I am busy” to anyone, or write it in a letter, often or without need; and not to keep excusing oneself in this way from the duties that come with one’s relations to those one lives among, by pleading the business that surrounds one.
members.greek: Παρὰ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Πλατωνικοῦ τὸ μὴ πολλάκις μηδὲ χωρὶς ἀνάγκης λέγειν πρός τινα ἢ ἐν ἐπιστολῇ γράφειν ὅτι ἄσχολός εἰμι, μηδὲ διὰ τούτου τοῦ τρόπου συνεχῶς παραιτεῖσθαι τὰ κατὰ τὰς πρὸς τοὺς συμβιοῦντας σχέσεις καθήκοντα, προβαλλόμενον τὰ περιεστῶτα πράγματα.

members.why: A note pointing at a story about Socrates in a sheepskin. Marcus does not give what Socrates said, and the story does not survive elsewhere.
members.text:
How Socrates looked, when he was fain to gird himself with a
skin, Xanthippe his wife having taken away his clothes, and carried them
abroad with her, and what he said to his fellows and friends, who were
ashamed; and out of respect to him, did retire themselves when they saw
him thus decked.
members.english: What Socrates was like with the sheepskin tied round his waist, when Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out; and what Socrates said to his companions, who were embarrassed and drew back when they saw him dressed like that.
members.greek: Οἷος ὁ Σωκράτης τὸ κῴδιον ὑπεζωσμένος, ὅτε ἡ Ξανθίππη λαβοῦσα τὸ ἱμάτιον ἔξω προῆλθε, καὶ ἃ εἶπεν ὁ Σωκράτης τοῖς ἑταίροις αἰδεσθεῖσι καὶ ἀναχωρήσασιν, ὅτε αὐτὸν εἶδον οὕτως ἐσταλμένον.

members.text:
Socrates was wont to call the common conceits and opinions of men,
the common bugbears of the world: the proper terror of silly children.
members.english: Socrates used to call the principles of the many, too, “Lamias”, things to frighten children.
members.greek: Σωκράτης καὶ τὰ τῶν πολλῶν δόγματα Λαμίας ἐκάλει, παιδίων δείματα.

members.text:
Of Fronto, to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a
tyrannous king is subject unto, and how they who are commonly called
εὐπατρίδαι, _i.e._ nobly born, are in some sort incapable, or void
of natural affection.
members.english: From Fronto: to have taken note of what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that on the whole these people we call patricians are somehow rather lacking in affection.
members.greek: Παρὰ Φρόντωνος τὸ ἐπιστῆσαι οἵα ἡ τυραννικὴ βασκανία καὶ ποικιλία καὶ ὑπόκρισις, καὶ ὅτι ὡς ἐπίπαν οἱ καλούμενοι οὗτοι παρ’ ἡμῖν εὐπατρίδαι ἀστοργότεροί πως εἰσί.

members.text:
Alexander of Macedon, and he that dressed his mules, when once
dead both came to one. For either they were both resumed into those
original rational essences from whence all things in the world are
propagated; or both after one fashion were scattered into atoms.
members.english: Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver, once dead, came to the same state: for either they were taken back into the same seed-reasons of the universe, or they were scattered alike into atoms.
members.greek: Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ Μακεδὼν καὶ ὁ ὀρεωκόμος αὐτοῦ ἀποθανόντες εἰς ταὐτὸ κατέστησαν· ἤτοι γὰρ ἀνελήφθησαν εἰς τοὺς αὐτοὺς τοῦ κόσμου σπερματικοὺς λόγους ἢ διεσκεδάσθησαν ὁμοίως εἰς τὰς ἀτόμους.

members.text:
From Alexander the Grammarian, to be un-reprovable myself, and not
reproachfully to reprehend any man for a barbarism, or a solecism, or
any false pronunciation, but dextrously by way of answer, or testimony,
or confirmation of the same matter (taking no notice of the word) to
utter it as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and
indirect admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.
members.english: From Alexander the grammarian: not to find fault, and not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with a wrong form of a word, a mistake in grammar or a jarring sound, but deftly to come out with just the very thing that should have been said, by way of an answer, or of backing them up, or of a joint discussion about the matter itself, not about the expression, or through some other such well-tuned reminder in passing.
members.greek: Παρὰ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ γραμματικοῦ τὸ ἀνεπίπληκτον καὶ τὸ μὴ ὀνειδιστικῶς ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι τῶν βάρβαρον ἢ σόλοικόν τι ἢ ἀπηχὲς προενεγκαμένων, ἀλλ’ ἐπιδεξίως αὐτὸ μόνον ἐκεῖνο ὃ ἔδει εἰρῆσθαι προφέρεσθαι ἐν τρόπῳ ἀποκρίσεως ἢ συνεπιμαρτυρήσεως ἢ συνδιαλήψεως περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πράγματος, οὐχὶ περὶ τοῦ ῥήματος, ἢ δι’ ἑτέρας τινὸς τοιαύτης ἐμμελοῦς παρυπομνήσεως.

members.why: One sentence cut from the end of a chapter: “See what Crates says about Xenocrates.” The saying itself is not given, so there is nothing to build on.
members.text: See what Crates pronounceth concerning Xenocrates himself.
members.english: See, at any rate, what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.
members.greek: ὅρα γοῦν ὁ Κράτης τί περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ξενοκράτους λέγει.

members.why: An example of hosts giving their visitors the better seats. Unlike 11.23 it gives no saying or reason in anyone’s words, and unlike 1.8 Marcus does not name it as something he learned; no other passage of the section speaks of guests.
members.text:
The Lacedæmonians at their public spectacles were wont to appoint
seats and forms for their strangers in the shadow, they themselves were
content to sit anywhere.
members.english: At their public shows the Spartans used to set the benches for foreign visitors in the shade, while they themselves sat wherever they happened to.
members.greek: Λακεδαιμόνιοι τοῖς μὲν ξένοις ἐν ταῖς θεωρίαις ὑπὸ τῇ σκιᾷ τὰ βάθρα ἐτίθεσαν, αὐτοὶ δὲ οὗ ἔτυχεν, ἐκαθέζοντο.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.26 is 7.44–48, 7.37 is 7.66–67a, 7.23 is 7.35, 11.23 is 11.25, 11.32 is 11.39, 1.9 is 1.12, 11.26 is 11.28, 11.21 is 11.23, 1.8 is 1.11, 6.22 is 6.24, 1.7 is 1.10, 6.12 is 6.13b and 11.22 is 11.24; 8.3 is the same.

Takes the words Marcus copied from Plato (the first three paragraphs of 7.26, and all of 7.23) as rules he holds himself. He copies them without comment; “A fine saying of Plato’s” is his only remark.

Reads 7.37’s list as the tests of a soul and uses three of them: just towards people and devout towards the gods, not idly angry at vice, not a slave to anyone’s ignorance. The other two, taking what the whole allots without complaint and not handing the mind over to the body, are left to Articles 3 and 2, which say them.

Uses two words of its own, “fame” and “power”, for the measures it rejects, in claim 2 and in the statement. “Power” is the larger step: 8.3 names Alexander, Gaius and Pompey and speaks of their slavery, not of their power.

Turns two descriptions into resolves: 8.3’s exclamation over the conquerors’ slavery into “I shall not be a slave”, and 7.23’s portrait of a mind with a view of all time into something I practise. Each is marked under the claim as the editor’s turn.
Places 6.22 under “If I doubt it”, as what holds whether the world is governed by reason or is only atoms. It does not say what holds if a person is not to be measured by the soul.

Sets aside three anecdotes that give neither a saying nor a reason: Socrates in the sheepskin (11.26), Crates on Xenocrates (6.12) and the Spartans’ benches (11.22). Socrates and Perdiccas (11.23) is kept because Socrates gives his reason in his own words, and Fronto’s lesson (1.8) because Marcus names it as one.
articles.limit: The section is a collection of sayings and examples, not one argument, and the article leans on two passages: 7.26 feeds three claims and 7.37 four, and claims 1 and 5 rest on the same pair, 7.26 and 7.23, both copied from Plato. Much of it is said in other articles: that I accept what the whole allots (Article 3), that the body’s feelings do not rule me (Article 2), that dying is nothing much and how long I live does not matter (Articles 17 and 35), that my one fear is of living against nature, not of ceasing to live (Article 10, claim 6, near claim 1 here), that being just is the one thing worth my effort (Articles 10 and 34), that I keep free of anger (Article 37), that I take the wide view, looking down on human affairs from high above and keeping all of eternity and all that exists in mind (Article 10, claim 5, and Article 32, claim 4, the same as claim 5 here; also Article 31), that I look into people’s ruling parts to see what they are (Article 27, claim 1, the same act as claim 2 here), that fame is nothing to me (Article 27), and that the dead are taken back or scattered alike (Articles 32 and 33). What this article adds is the measure of a person, the soul and not fame or power, with the judgment that dying is not the worst thing set beside it.

claims.t: Staying alive is not the great thing, and I do not cling to life or count death terrible. Where I have taken up a post, judging it best, or been posted there, I stay and run the risk. I take nothing into account ahead of disgrace, not even death.
claims.shared: Restores the post “judged best” or assigned, and the source’s “ahead of disgrace” in place of “shameful”. The post is a single-source detail from 7.26. Limit: 7.26 hedges with “perhaps” and 7.23 is conditional on a great mind.

support.follows: What is noble and good may be something other than staying alive, and perhaps a true man must let go of how long he lives.

claims.t: I look at what kind of soul a person has. I ask what Alexander, Gaius and Pompey are beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates, who saw things, their causes and their matter. A more glorious death and nimbler argument do not prove that Socrates was better than Telauges.
claims.shared: Removes the unsupported “hardly anyone has heard of him” and the verdict “little”. Both comparisons stay as the questions the sources ask. The Telauges question is from 7.37 alone and is not a verdict against Socrates.

support.quote: what has to be looked at is this: what kind of soul Socrates had
support.follows: The thing to look at in Socrates is what kind of soul he had.
gives: I look at what kind of soul a person has

support.quote: For the latter saw things and their causes and their matter, and their ruling parts were the same.
support.follows: The reason given for setting the philosophers higher is what they saw and the state of their ruling parts.
gives: I look at what kind of soul a person has
who saw things, their causes and their matter

support.quote: Alexander, Gaius and Pompey: what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates?
support.follows: Alexander, Gaius and Pompey amount to little when set beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates.

support.quote: it is not enough that Socrates died a more glorious death, and argued more nimbly with the sophists
support.follows: A more glorious death and more skill in argument are not enough to show that Socrates was the better man.
gives: A more glorious death and nimbler argument do not prove

support.quote: How do we know that Telauges was not better than Socrates in his disposition?
support.follows: We do not know that Telauges was not the better man in his inner disposition.
gives: that Socrates was better than Telauges

claims.t: When I act I look at this alone: whether I am doing what is just or unjust, the deeds of a good person or of a bad one. I find it enough to be just in my dealings with people and devout in my dealings with the gods.
claims.shared: Keeps the source wording and restores the good and bad deeds. Limit: in 7.37 “enough” is a test put to Socrates’ soul, adopted here as my own standard. Devotion to the gods is from 7.37 alone.

support.quote: look at this alone whenever he acts: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one
support.follows: Whenever a man acts he should look at one thing only: whether what he is doing is just or unjust.

whether I am doing what is just or unjust, the deeds of a good person or of a bad one

support.quote: whether he could find it enough to be just in his dealings with human beings and devout in his dealings with the gods
support.follows: The question about Socrates is whether being just to people and devout to the gods was enough for him.
gives: I find it enough to be just in my dealings with people
devout in my dealings with the gods

claims.t: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong. I do not get idly angry at vice, and I do not pounce reproachfully on a wrong word or a slip of grammar. If we say we have sound souls, I ask why we fight and fall out.
claims.shared: The existing line vowed not to quarrel, but 11.32 ends on a question, so the question stands. “Souls” is supplied from the fuller exchange in 11.32. 1.7 covers errors of language only and is named as such.

support.quote: neither getting idly angry at vice
support.follows: The soul this passage asks about does not get angry at vice to no purpose.

support.quote: not to find fault, and not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with a wrong form of a word, a mistake in grammar or a jarring sound

support.quote: “Sound ones.” “Then why do you not look for them?” “Because we have them.” “Then why do you fight and fall out?”

claims.t: I take the wide view of all time and all being. When I speak of human beings, I look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above. I look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and I think continually of the elements changing into one another. These impressions wash away the dirt of life on the ground.
claims.shared: Removes the semicolon and restores “running round with them” and the condition about speaking of human beings. The star and dirt images are from 7.26 alone. The view cleanses and does not express contempt.

support.quote: a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of all being

of all time and all being

support.quote: whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above
support.follows: Anyone who talks about human beings should also look down at earthly things as if from above.

claims.t: I guard against slavery of two kinds. One is to be a slave to anyone’s ignorance. The other is to have many things to take thought for and to be a slave to many.
claims.shared: The existing vow named the three commanders, but this claim’s quote from 8.3 says only “the others”, so the names stay in c2. The observation is kept as a guard, not a vow. Each kind of slavery has one witness.

support.quote: nor yet being a slave to anyone’s ignorance
support.follows: The soul this passage asks about is not a slave to anyone’s ignorance.
gives: I guard against slavery
a slave to anyone’s ignorance

support.quote: But with the others, how many things to take thought for, and slavery to how many!
